tldr: A planner-free reinforcement-learning controller that directly incorporates a spatial bias based on semantic costs into its attention mechanism, enabling legged robots to simultaneously reason about where they can physically step and where they must not step (such as pipes or grass).
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed SABER method. A terrain-affordance map (3D geometry + contact cost) is tokenized with a CNN, and cross-attention is applied using proprioceptive queries that include per-foot kinematics. The contact cost is not only passed to the CNN input, but also directly added to the attention logits as a distance-dependent semantic bias from the feet.
overview:
Recent quadrupedal robots use reinforcement learning to read terrain variations directly from depth sensors or elevation maps. This allows them to agilely traverse rugged terrain, stairs, and parkour courses. However, conventional controllers essentially only look at "geometric information (surface shape)." In industrial environments, pipes, fragile cardboard boxes, or slippery grass may geometrically look like flat, traversable footholds, but they are hazardous areas where the robot must not step.

In existing systems, semantics were handled either by having high-level planners detour around entire areas, or by relying on post-hoc recovery after the robot stepped through soft ground. If a robot must step over an obstacle that geometrically resembles a stepping stone, the low-level locomotion policy itself must understand "do not step here." Otherwise, it risks planting its foot straight onto the forbidden hazard.

To solve this, this paper proposes SABER, a reinforcement-learning policy where the low-level controller itself jointly reasons about geometry and contact permission without a planner. Each cell in a local map carries a contact cost, and a learned bias conditioned on the distance to each foot is directly injected into the cross-attention logits. Simulation evaluations show that simply removing this bias causes forbidden contacts to jump by 55%. Furthermore, real-world tests on a Unitree B2 demonstrate that the robot accurately distinguishes and selects footholds across unseen pipes, cardboard boxes, and grass.
contributions: Introduced a "terrain-affordance map" combining 3D terrain coordinates with semantic contact costs, decoupling where the robot can step from where it should step at foothold resolution.
Proposed a "structured semantic attention bias" mechanism that adjusts attention weights with a learned, signed term on logits based on the distance from the nearest foot.
Designed a training environment that intentionally decorrelates terrain geometry from contact costs, learning a robust contact selection policy that does not overfit to shape alone.
Implemented the policy onboard a physical Unitree B2, demonstrating direct sim-to-real transfer across four semantic obstacle classes in indoor and outdoor environments.

sections.heading: Can it be stepped on? vs. Should it be stepped on?
sections.summary: Conventional quadruped locomotion policies focus almost entirely on terrain shape (elevation changes), unable to distinguish "obstacles that are physically traversable but must not be contacted," such as pipes or fragile boxes. This work solves this problem by introducing a semantic affordance map directly usable by a low-level controller alongside a foot-distance-aware attention bias mechanism.
sections.details:
Legged locomotion control has advanced rapidly from blind traversal over rough terrain to predictive control using exteroceptive sensors, and further to acrobatic behaviors like stairs and parkour. However, most terrain representations used here are limited to geometric information such as "height" or "elevation changes."

This introduces a fundamental issue. Geometry tells the robot whether a foothold exists, but it does not convey contact permission—whether the foot is allowed to touch it. In an industrial plant, a narrow pipe or a fragile payload looks like a solid step geometrically, so a conventional controller treats it as an ideal foothold and steps right on it. Conversely, grass patches or shallow puddles look flat, yet they are slippery spots the robot should avoid.

In traditional navigation systems, a high-level planner builds a semantic cost map and detours around the entire region. However, when the robot must step directly over an obstacle, accidents will happen unless the low-level locomotion controller itself can decide "do not step here; place the foot in this gap." A key feature of SABER is that it handles this decision entirely within an end-to-end reinforcement-learning policy, without relying on an external step planner.

captions.F1: Semantic contact selection on a real Unitree B2. In the terrain-affordance map on the left, pipe cells are labeled as forbidden ($r=1$, red). The robot selects only safe footholds of similar shape, stepping over the pipe without making contact.

sections.heading: Prior limitations: High-level detours or post-impact recovery
sections.summary: Most prior studies used only geometric inputs to avoid the sim-to-real gap of visual textures. Even when semantics were considered, they were limited to speed adaptations or coarse path detours; no policy directly accounted for semantic costs at the low-level foot-placement level.
sections.details:
### Geometry-focused learning-based locomotion
Many reinforcement-learning policies rely on robot-centric elevation maps or egocentric depth images. Because visual textures and color images suffer from a large sim-to-real gap, sticking strictly to simulatable geometry has been the standard practice. However, the cost of this approach is that when encountering compliant terrain like snow, grass, or foam—which can only be detected after stepping on it—the robot can only recover its posture post-hoc after the foot sinks. Recent agile locomotion work has focused on sharpening geometric awareness, such as penalizing footholds on sharp edges, leaving semantic contact decisions largely unexplored.

### Attention mechanisms in locomotion
An increasing number of studies (such as AME) tokenize depth image patches or local elevation maps and select footholds using transformer attention. However, existing methods rely either on standard dot-product scoring between queries and keys or on static kinematically driven masks. No locomotion policy had yet incorporated a learned additive logit bias for spatial contact semantics, similar to relative position encodings used in natural language processing.

### Semantic integration and its challenges
There have been attempts to bring semantics into legged robotics, but most simply let a high-level path planner route around high-cost regions while the low-level controller only sees geometry. In the few works that considered semantics at the foothold level (such as SemLoco), an external heuristic search decided the footholds, rather than the policy itself selecting them directly inside its attention mechanism.

sections.heading: SABER's architecture: Weighting hazard by distance to the foot
sections.summary: SABER takes a 4-channel map combining 3D terrain coordinates and contact-forbidden flags, tokenizing it with a lightweight CNN. During cross-attention with queries containing foot positions and velocities, a learned bias conditioned on the distance from the nearest foot is added to the logits, selectively suppressing hazardous cells near the stepping foot.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B Terrain-affordance map and tokenization
The policy represents a $2.0\,\mathrm{m} \times 1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ area centered in front of the robot as a grid with $0.05\,\mathrm{m}$ resolution ($41 \times 21$ cells). Each cell contains local 3D coordinates $[x, y, z]$ and a contact cost $r \in \{0, 1\}$. Here, $r=1$ marks a "flagged cell" that must not be stepped on. These inputs pass through a lightweight 2-layer CNN, producing $21 \times 11$ (231 total) 64-dimensional terrain tokens. Because the coordinates are provided directly as channels, no separate positional encoding needs to be added.

### III-C Structured semantic attention bias
Simply mixing geometry and cost in the CNN input risks diluting the cost signal through successive convolutions. Therefore, SABER introduces a bypass path in the 8-head cross-attention that adds a bias term directly to the pre-softmax logits.

The attention score for each head $h$ is computed as $S_h = (Q_h K_h^T)/\sqrt{d_h} + B_h$. Here, the bias $B_h$ is defined as the product of a per-head gain $\beta_h$, a radial distance profile $\rho_h(d)$ relative to the foot, and the per-token cost $\bar{r}$. Each cell is assigned the horizontal distance $d$ to the nearest foot, and a piecewise-linear function $\rho_h(d)$ modulates the influence across distances. This allows individual heads to learn to strongly attend to hazards right near the stepping foot while ignoring distant ones.

### III-D Training pipeline and environment design
The policy is trained end-to-end with an asymmetric Actor-Critic setup using PPO. The design of the training terrain is critical here. If every elevated pipe is labeled contact-forbidden, the policy will avoid obstacles purely based on geometric height, ignoring the cost channel altogether. To prevent this, the training environment includes "traversable pipes and rails" as well as "flat but forbidden grass and lava tiles," completely breaking the correlation between geometry and contact permission.

captions.F3: The six terrain types used for training: rough terrain, pipes, stepping stones, rails, lava tiles, and grass rings. Even for identical geometries, forbidden cells (red dots) and safe cells (blue dots) are mixed, forcing the policy not to rely on shape alone.

sections.heading: Removing the bias increases contacts by 55%! Sim and real validation
sections.summary: Ablation experiments showed that removing the attention bias alone increased forbidden contacts by 55%. Furthermore, on a real Unitree B2, combining a LiDAR elevation map with camera-based YOLO segmentation demonstrated that the robot successfully avoids pipes, cardboard boxes, and grass patches.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation results and ablations
SABER and several baselines with removed components were evaluated across five challenging terrain types.
- In the model without semantic bias (w/o bias), velocity tracking error and traversal distance remained unchanged, but forbidden contacts per episode jumped by 55%.
- In the geometry-only model where the semantic channel was completely removed, contacts reached 13.5 per episode (roughly 13 times SABER), blindly trampling over hazardous regions.
- On "lava tiles," "grass rings," and "stepping stones," where geometric cues are completely absent, the presence or absence of the semantic bias produced the most pronounced difference.
- Visualizing the internal attention bias revealed that 7 out of 8 heads suppressed attention weights on hazardous cells. In particular, right before touchdown, attention sharply concentrated on the target landing cells.

### IV-B Real-world validation (Unitree B2)
A single policy checkpoint from simulation was deployed directly onto a Unitree B2 quadruped robot. The system builds real-time affordance maps onboard by combining LiDAR-based state estimation and elevation mapping with camera-based YOLOv8 segmentation (detecting grass, plants, pipes, and boxes).
- Indoor experiment: In a stepping-stone setup with safe concrete blocks and forbidden cardboard boxes of identical height and dimensions, the robot stepped only on the concrete blocks while skillfully avoiding the cardboard.
- Outdoor experiment: On a sidewalk with alternating stone pavers and grass slits, enabling semantics caused the robot to place its feet exclusively on the narrow stones. Disabling semantics caused it to step directly onto the grass without hesitation.

captions.F4: Contact count comparison across three terrains with no geometric cues (stepping stones, grass rings, lava tiles). SABER (blue) incurs substantially fewer contacts compared to the model without bias (gray).
captions.F7: Analysis of the learned semantic attention bias. (a) Effective bias values per head plotted against distance $d$ to the nearest foot. A strong suppression peak (negative logit) appears around $0.45\,\mathrm{m}$. (b) The bias reduces attention mass on forbidden cells by about 3 percentage points across all terrains.
captions.F8: Real-world comparison on an outdoor stone-paver walkway with grass slits. (a) With semantics enabled, the robot accurately selects narrow stone footholds (solid red circles). (b) With semantics disabled, it steps straight onto flat grass patches (dashed red circles).

sections.heading: Toward a new standard for semantics in locomotion control
sections.summary: SABER shows that a low-level locomotion policy can reason directly about semantic affordances at foothold resolution. Future challenges include handling real-world segmentation noise and map drift, as well as extending the approach to other platforms like humanoids.
sections.details:
This paper establishes SABER, a legged locomotion controller that simultaneously reasons about semantic contact permissions and terrain geometry without relying on an external planner. Through the simple combination of a terrain-affordance map and a foot-distance-dependent signed attention bias, the policy autonomously discriminates between "permitted" and "forbidden" footholds at the foot-placement level, even when geometries are identical.

Current limitations include susceptibility to geometric misalignments when projecting 2D camera segmentations onto 2.5D elevation maps, as well as map drift during sharp turns or rapid motions. Furthermore, because learned constraints are enforced via soft RL penalties, commanding the robot forward when no safe footholds exist can still cause it to step into forbidden zones. Future work includes incorporating semantic uncertainty into training, exploring end-to-end egocentric visual representations without intermediate metric mapping, and applying the approach to humanoid robots.

takeaways: "Where a robot can step (geometry)" and "where it should step (semantics)" are fundamentally distinct and must be explicitly separated at the input stage of low-level locomotion policies.
Adding a learned, distance-conditioned logit bias to transformer cross-attention enables selective suppression of hazardous areas strictly within the spatial range where foot placement matters.
Decoupling shape from meaning in simulation—such as mixing traversable and non-traversable pipes—is key to preventing the policy from overfitting to geometric cues.
Without running an expensive high-level planner, a well-designed attention mechanism enables an end-to-end low-level RL policy to handle foothold selection on its own.
limitations: Relies on projecting 2D camera segmentation onto a 2.5D elevation map, making it vulnerable to calibration errors, map drift, and misclassifications.

Semantic constraints are learned through soft reinforcement learning penalties, meaning aggressive velocity commands can still force the robot into forbidden zones when no safe footholds are available.
Contact costs are currently represented as a binary (0 or 1) mask, without capturing continuous degrees of slipperiness or structural fragility.
